title: What is Kafka Connect — a tool to move data INTO Kafka (Source Connectors) and OUT OF Kafka (Sink Connectors) without writing code — for example, a JDBC Source Connector reads database tables and writes them as Kafka topics, and an S3 Sink Connector writes Kafka topics to S3 files?
shortTitle: What is Kafka Connect, and how do source and sink connectors move data in and out of Kafka without code?

s1_definition.profdef: Kafka Connect is a framework and runtime for streaming data between Kafka and external systems using configuration instead of custom code. A Source Connector pulls data from an external system into Kafka topics, and a Sink Connector pushes data from Kafka topics out to an external system. You deploy a pre-built connector, give it a JSON configuration describing the external system and the topics, and Connect handles the running, scaling, offset tracking, and fault tolerance. For example, a JDBC Source Connector reads rows from database tables and produces them as Kafka records, while an S3 Sink Connector consumes Kafka records and writes them as files in object storage.
s1_definition.analogy: Kafka Connect is like hiring a specialised courier service at National Bank of India instead of training your own messengers. A source courier knows exactly how to walk into the account database, copy out new rows, and drop them into the Kafka sorting office. A sink courier knows how to take sorted messages out of the Kafka office and file them neatly into cloud storage. You never teach the couriers how to drive; you just fill out a form saying which building to visit and what to carry, and the courier company handles vehicles, backups if one breaks down, and remembering exactly where it left off.
s1_definition.oneliner: Kafka Connect moves data into Kafka with source connectors and out of Kafka with sink connectors, all by configuration and with no custom code.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Kafka Connect is a framework and runtime for streaming data between Kafka and external systems using configuration instead of custom code. A Source Connector pulls data from an external system into Kafka topics, and a Sink Connector pushes data from Kafka topics out to an external system. You deploy a pre-built connector, give it a JSON configuration describing the external system and the topics, and Connect handles the running, scaling, offset tracking, and fault tolerance. For example, a JDBC Source Connector reads rows from database tables and produces them as Kafka records, while an S3 Sink Connector consumes Kafka records and writes them as files in object storage.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Kafka Connect is like hiring a specialised courier service at National Bank of India instead of training your own messengers. A source courier knows exactly how to walk into the account database, copy out new rows, and drop them into the Kafka sorting office. A sink courier knows how to take sorted messages out of the Kafka office and file them neatly into cloud storage. You never teach the couriers how to drive; you just fill out a form saying which building to visit and what to carry, and the courier company handles vehicles, backups if one breaks down, and remembering exactly where it left off.

**One line to remember:** Kafka Connect moves data into Kafka with source connectors and out of Kafka with sink connectors, all by configuration and with no custom code.

sections.s2_technical:
The core idea is that most data movement between Kafka and other systems is repetitive plumbing: connect, read or write in batches, track position, retry on failure, scale out. Kafka Connect packages that plumbing once so you only supply configuration. You pick a connector that already knows a specific system, give it a configuration, and submit it to the Connect runtime, which then runs it continuously. There is no producer or consumer code to write, build, or deploy for the common cases.

A Source Connector imports data into Kafka. The JDBC Source Connector is the classic example: you configure the database connection, a table or query, and a mode such as polling for new rows by an incrementing id or a timestamp column, and Connect reads the new rows and produces them as records into a Kafka topic, one topic per table by convention. It remembers how far it has read using source offsets stored in Kafka, so after a restart it resumes from the last imported row instead of re-importing everything. Other source connectors read files, message queues, or change-data-capture logs.

A Sink Connector exports data out of Kafka. The S3 Sink Connector is the classic example: you configure the bucket, the topics to consume, the file format, and a flush policy, and Connect consumes the records and writes them as files to object storage, committing Kafka consumer offsets only after the files are safely written so nothing is lost. Other sink connectors write to relational databases, Elasticsearch, or data warehouses. In both directions, Connect manages the Kafka side of offsets automatically, so you get reliable, resumable movement without hand-written commit logic.

The value is speed and reliability for standard integrations. A JDBC source plus an S3 sink can build an entire pipeline from an operational database to a data lake with two configuration files and zero application code, and the Connect runtime gives you scaling by splitting the work into tasks across workers, fault tolerance by restarting failed tasks on healthy workers, and consistent offset handling. The senior nuances are that Connect is ideal when a pre-built connector exists and the transformation needed is light, using Single Message Transforms for small tweaks; that for heavy, stateful processing you still reach for a stream-processing application; that converters decide the on-the-wire format, so you choose JSON, Avro, or Protobuf and often pair Avro with a schema registry; and that Connect's at-least-once default means sink targets should be idempotent or deduplicating, though some sinks support exactly-once.
sections.s3_banking:
The real problem at National Bank of India is that account data living in the operational database needs to reach both a real-time stream and a long-term archive, and the team does not want to hand-write and maintain producers and consumers for each.

Problem 1 — the analytics team wants every new account and every balance change from the accounts table to appear in Kafka continuously, without the core banking developers writing a custom producer. This is exactly what a JDBC Source Connector solves: point it at the accounts table, and new rows flow into a Kafka topic automatically.

Problem 2 — the compliance team needs every message in that topic archived as files in cloud object storage for seven years, and nobody wants to maintain a bespoke consumer that writes files and tracks offsets. This is exactly what an S3 Sink Connector solves: point it at the topic and the bucket, and records become archived files reliably.

Problem 3 — both must survive restarts without re-importing or losing data. This is exactly what Connect's offset management provides: the source resumes from the last imported row and the sink commits offsets only after files are written.

The code will model a `JdbcSourceConnector` that polls an accounts table for new rows and produces them to a topic, a Kafka topic stand-in, and an `S3SinkConnector` that consumes the topic and writes files, both driven purely by a configuration object with no bespoke producer or consumer logic. The demo step is: insert account rows for Rajesh and Priya, run the source to import them, run the sink to archive them, then restart and show both resuming from their saved offsets.

##### 4b. SQL Database Script

```sql
-- V1__create_tables.sql (source of truth the JDBC Source Connector reads)
CREATE TABLE accounts (
    id          BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,       -- incrementing id: source polling column
    account_no  VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    holder_name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    balance     DECIMAL(15,2) NOT NULL
);

INSERT INTO accounts (id, account_no, holder_name, balance) VALUES
    (1, 'SAV2001', 'Rajesh Kumar', 1000000.00),
    (2, 'CUR3001', 'Priya Sharma', 250000.00);
```

##### 4c. Configuration File

```yaml
# connectors/jdbc-source.json (submitted to Connect REST API — NO code)
# {
#   "name": "accounts-jdbc-source",
#   "config": {
#     "connector.class": "io.confluent.connect.jdbc.JdbcSourceConnector",
#     "connection.url": "jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/bankdb",
#     "table.whitelist": "accounts",
#     "mode": "incrementing",
#     "incrementing.column.name": "id",
#     "topic.prefix": "bank."
#   }
# }

# connectors/s3-sink.json
# {
#   "name": "accounts-s3-sink",
#   "config": {
#     "connector.class": "io.confluent.connect.s3.S3SinkConnector",
#     "topics": "bank.accounts",
#     "s3.bucket.name": "nbi-account-archive",
#     "format.class": "io.confluent.connect.s3.format.json.JsonFormat",
#     "flush.size": "2"
#   }
# }
```

```bash
javac com/bank/connect/demo/ConnectDemo.java
java com.bank.connect.demo.ConnectDemo

# In a real Kafka Connect deployment (no application code at all):
curl -X POST http://localhost:8083/connectors -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d @connectors/jdbc-source.json
curl -X POST http://localhost:8083/connectors -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d @connectors/s3-sink.json
curl http://localhost:8083/connectors/accounts-jdbc-source/status
```
sections.s5_journey:
The input is an accounts table containing Rajesh and Priya, which must flow into Kafka and then out to cloud storage, all by configuration.

Step 1: The JDBC Source Connector polls the accounts table. Its source offset starts at zero, so it reads all rows with an id greater than zero, meaning both Rajesh at id one and Priya at id two.

Step 2: The connector produces each row as a JSON record into the Kafka topic and advances its source offset to two. No producer code was written; the connector did it from configuration.

Step 3: The S3 Sink Connector consumes the topic from its own offset of zero, finds two records, and writes them as a single file in the bucket because the flush size is two, then commits its offset to two only after the file is safely written.

Step 4: A new account for Amit at id three is inserted into the table. On the next poll the source connector reads only rows with an id greater than its saved offset of two, so it imports just id three and does not re-import Rajesh or Priya.

Step 5: The sink consumes from its saved offset of two, finds the one new record, writes it to a second file, and commits its offset to three.

Step 6: The final state shows three records in the topic and two files in the bucket, with both connectors having resumed cleanly from their saved offsets after the new data arrived.

```
2026-10-24 23:26:40 [INFO] === source imports new DB rows INTO Kafka (no code) ===
2026-10-24 23:26:40 [INFO] source imported id=1 -> topic bank.accounts
2026-10-24 23:26:40 [INFO] source imported id=2 -> topic bank.accounts
2026-10-24 23:26:40 [INFO] === sink exports Kafka records OUT to S3 files (no code) ===
2026-10-24 23:26:40 [INFO] wrote s3://nbi-account-archive/accounts-1.json with 2 records
2026-10-24 23:26:40 [INFO] sink committed offset=2 (file flushed first)
2026-10-24 23:26:40 [INFO] === add a new row, restart: both resume from saved offsets ===
2026-10-24 23:26:40 [INFO] source imported id=3 -> topic bank.accounts
2026-10-24 23:26:40 [INFO] wrote s3://nbi-account-archive/accounts-2.json with 1 records
2026-10-24 23:26:40 [INFO] sink committed offset=3 (file flushed first)
2026-10-24 23:26:40 [INFO] topic size=3 s3 files=2
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  accounts table (external source)
    id=1 Rajesh, id=2 Priya, (later) id=3 Amit
    │
    ▼  JDBC Source Connector (config only; source offset = last id)
  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │ Kafka topic: bank.accounts    │ ← records flow IN
  │ [row1][row2]...[row3]          │
  └──────────────┬────────────────┘

  │ accounts-2.json (1 row)        │
  └──────────────────────────────┘
  Restart: source resumes from last id, sink resumes from committed offset
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Source + Sink Connector Design ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Adapter: each connector adapts an external system to Kafka records │
  │   WHY: one framework, many systems, zero bespoke glue code        │
  │ Template Method: poll()/put() skeletons provided by Connect        │
  │   WHY: connector authors fill in reads/writes only                │
  │ Checkpoint (offsets): source offset + sink offset for resumability │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: source imports; sink exports; topic transports                 │
  │ O: new system = new connector config, no change to the pipeline    │
  │ D: pipeline depends on connector abstractions, not on JDBC/S3 SDKs │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──────────────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌──────────────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │ JdbcSourceConnector      │───────▶│ KafkaTopic                │
  │ - sourceOffsetLastId     │ append │ + append/from/size        │
  │ + poll()                 │        └───────────┬──────────────┘
  └──────────────────────────┘                    │ consumed by
  ┌──────────────────────────┐                    ▼
  │ S3SinkConnector          │        ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │ - sinkOffset             │───────▶│ S3Bucket                  │
  │ - flushSize              │ write  │ + writeFile / fileCount   │
  │ + consume()              │        └──────────────────────────┘
  └──────────────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: a source connector ──────────────────────────────

  [STARTED offset=0] ──poll──→ [IMPORTED offset=2] ──new row──→ [IMPORTED offset=3]
       │ restart                    │ restart                      │
       └── resume from saved offset ┘ (never re-imports old rows) ─┘

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ─────────────────────────────────────

  1. source.poll() → import id 1,2 → topic size 2, source offset 2
  2. sink.consume() → write file (2 rows) → sink offset 2
  3. db.insert(id 3)
  4. source.poll() → import only id 3 → topic size 3
  5. sink.consume() → write file (1 row) → sink offset 3
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Kafka Connect is a framework and runtime for streaming data between Kafka and external systems using configuration instead of custom code. The whole point is that moving data in and out of Kafka is repetitive plumbing, connect, read or write in batches, track position, retry, and scale, and Connect packages that once so I only supply a JSON configuration and submit it to the runtime. There are two directions: a source connector pulls data from an external system into Kafka topics, and a sink connector pushes data from Kafka topics out to an external system.

The canonical examples make it concrete. A JDBC source connector reads rows from database tables, polling by an incrementing id or a timestamp, and produces them as records into a topic, one topic per table, remembering how far it has read with source offsets so it resumes after a restart instead of re-importing everything. An S3 sink connector consumes a topic and writes the records as files in object storage, committing the Kafka consumer offsets only after the files are safely written, so nothing is lost.

In the account pipeline at National Bank of India this let us connect the operational accounts database to a real-time stream and a long-term archive with two configuration files and no application code. A JDBC source streamed every new account and balance change into a Kafka topic for the analytics team, and an S3 sink archived that topic as files for compliance, and both survived restarts because Connect manages their offsets, the source resuming from the last imported row and the sink committing only after each file was written.

The senior nuances I add are that Connect shines when a pre-built connector exists and the transformation is light, where I can use single-message transforms for small tweaks, while heavy stateful processing still belongs in a stream-processing application; that converters choose the wire format, so I pick JSON, Avro, or Protobuf and often pair Avro with a schema registry; and that Connect is at-least-once by default, so sink targets should be idempotent or deduplicating, although some connectors support exactly-once. The runtime also gives me scaling by splitting work into tasks across workers and fault tolerance by restarting failed tasks, all without me writing or operating producers and consumers.
